newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian parliament claims artworks as spoils of WW2.
newsitem.headline: Russian parliament claims artworks as spoils of WW2.

text.p: Russia's parliament on Wednesday approved a draft law laying claim to art treasures seized from Nazi Germany during World War Two, including paintings by Matisse and Cezanne.
The lower house passed the draft law on so-called "Trophy art" by 291 votes to one.
"All art valuables brought to the Soviet Union as a result of World War Two...are owned by the Russian Federation and are recognised as federal property," it said.

The new law, drawn up following recommendations from a joint commission of both houses of parliament, differs little from previous legislation which limited the conditions under which war booty could be returned.

Many Russians view the treasures, seized from museums and private homes in Germany and its wartime allies, as Russian -- compensation for the wartime suffering of the Soviet Union and the destruction of many of its own treasures at Nazi hands.
The Federation Council upper house rejected a first draft law last July, saying approval of the document would harm international relations.
Germany, anxious for the return of the treasures, has argued that Russia is obliged under existing treaties to hand the artworks back. An embassy official declined to comment on the latest decision.
"This is a sensitive problem being discussed at the highest levels and a reaction would come from Bonn and not from the embassy," he said.
The legislation must still be approved by the Federation Council and signed into law by President Boris Yeltsin, who is recovering from pneumonia at an official residence outside Moscow.
The parliament's approval of the original law on trophy art dismayed many German politicians, who described it as an "unfriendly act".
Itar-Tass news agency quoted Russian Deputy Culture Minister Mikhail Shvydkoi as saying that the law could have serious international consequences.

"I have serious doubts about this law," he said. "The Duma (lower house) has gone ahead and passed it, virtually in its original format, regardless of our suggestions on how it could be dramatically improved."
Germany said the row centred on 200,000 works of art worth billions of marks (dollars). They include dozens of priceless paintings and a golden hoard from ancient Troy currently on display in Moscow.
The Soviet Union complained that officials handed over around two million works of art up to the 1990s, but received only a handful of works back in return.

The legislation approved on Wednesday gives some former Soviet republics, including the Baltic states of Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania, the right to claim back artworks brought to Russia during the war if they had received no compensation for their own losses from Germany or Germany's war allies.
